newsitem.title: UK: Reed down on downgrade, U.S. court ruling.
newsitem.headline: Reed down on downgrade, U.S. court ruling.

text.p: Shares in Reed International Plc dropped sharply in on Thursday as analysts at Merrill Lynch downgraded the stock and a U.S. press report raised concerns about the group's U.S. legal publishing unit Lexis-Nexis, dealers said.

A report in the New York Times said a Federal judge had removed much of the copyright protection claimed by leading legal publishing group West Publishing. The paper said the ruling was expected to drive down the price of legal research in the United States.
Reed shares were down 22p at 603-1/2 by 0943 GMT in volume of 3.8 million shares.
The New York Times report said West's law books and its electronic versions had become so valuable that last June the Thomson Corporation had paid $1.4 billion for the company.
But it said the ruling meant that rival publishers can electronically scan decision in West law books into their computers and then issue them in book, on-line or CD-ROM form.
Under the ruling, only West's notes and other added material are protected.
Reed, which paid $1.5 billion for Lexis-Nexis in 1994, said it had no immediate comment on the ruling.
A Reuters report said Mathew Bender & Co Inc had sued West, challenging the extent of its copyright protection with respect to the opinions of the U.S. Supreme Court and the federal appeals courts.
The ruling was handed down on Monday by Judge John Martin Jr of Federal District Court in Manhattan.
Hyperlaw Inc, a publisher of CD-ROM products including one that contains recent Supreme Court cases and one that contains recent appeals court cases, joined the lawsuit as a plaintiff.
Hyperlaw obtains some of the cases in its publications by scanning the title, text and certain other information directly from West's texts.
Martin ruled that Hyperlaw is entitled to copy opinions from the West texts, the court documents showed.
Earlier market sources said analysts at Merrill Lynch had lowered the stock to "accumulate" from "buy" following a briefing with executives from the company, dealers said.
There was market talk that at least one other major brokerage was also planning to lower its earnings expectations for the media and publishing group.
However it was not clear of the downgrades were directly related to the U.S. court ruling and analysts at the two brokerages were not immediately available for comment.
The New York Times said Thomson planned to appeal against the ruling. -- David Holmes, London Newsroom +44 171 542 4367
